title: Halloween pack 01: 6 spooky animal myths (Shorts v2)
_note: Mayor's seasonal order (2026-10-24), to post 10/28-10/31. Suggested slots: 10/28 crow + spider eggs, 10/29 owl, 10/30 black widow, 10/31 vampire bat + black cat (biggest searches on the day). Persona and v2 rules as the series pack; fun-spooky, no gore (no dead-animal or feeding photos). Dropped from the Mayor's list: 'bats are blind' (already posted, myths-01-short-bat) and 'wolves howl at the moon' (no CC0/CC BY howling-wolf photo on iNaturalist whose first photo shows howling; the renderer pins photos[0] only). Replaced with 'black widows eat their mates'. SCRIPTS ONLY until the new rig is approved; if the rig slips past 10/28, render these on the current rig rather than miss the date (Mayor's call). 'shot' is the pending Studio shot grammar.

beats.say: Vampire bats don't suck blood. They make a tiny cut, and lap it up with their tongue.
beats.short_title: Vampire Bats Don't Suck Blood (They Do Something Weirder) 🦇
beats.bonus: A vampire bat can die after about 70 hours without a meal, which is why roostmates share.
beats.comment: Creepier or cuter than you thought? 👇
sources: Vampire bats cut and lap with a grooved tongue; saliva numbs and keeps blood flowing — https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/151117-vampire-bats-blood-food-science-animals
Draculin, anticoagulant glycoprotein in Desmodus rotundus saliva, named after Count Dracula (Fernandez et al. 1998, Thromb. Haemost.) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draculin
Wilkinson 1984, Nature, 'Reciprocal food sharing in the vampire bat' (regurgitated blood shared with roostmates) — https://socialbat.org/2016/07/01/revisiting-wilkinson-1984
Common vampire bats feed mainly on livestock (cattle, horses); people rarely — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_vampire_bat
Photo note: 248835378 shows a gloved hand at the left edge; crops start right of it.

beats.say: Their spit has a blood thinner called draculin. Yes. After Dracula.
And a bat that missed dinner gets a shared meal from a roostmate.
They share dinner. I have only ever been dinner.
They don't suck. They lap. Mostly cows, not you.
Black widows usually don't eat their mates. In the western black widow, it's never been seen in the wild.
beats.loop_say: Most males just leave. Quietly. Smart. Because
beats.short_title: Black Widows Usually Don't Eat Their Mates 🕷️
beats.bonus: In a few Southern Hemisphere widow species, eating the male is the norm. Not this one.
beats.comment: Who told you the black widow always eats the male? 👇
sources: Burke Museum spider myths (Rod Crawford), 'Myth: Black widows eat their mates': never observed in the wild for L. hesperus; old data from lab cages where males couldn't escape; females weigh 10-160x males — https://www.burkemuseum.org/blog/myth-black-widows-eat-their-mates
LiveScience, black widow facts (females do not usually eat mates) — https://www.livescience.com/39919-black-widow-spiders.html
Photos are all Latrodectus hesperus (western black widow), the species the hook names.

beats.say: The old stories came from lab cages, where the male couldn't escape.
She can weigh up to a hundred and sixty times what he does.
Small guest, big eater's house. Leave early. Leave politely.
Not always eaten. Mostly just awkward.
Black cats aren't bad luck everywhere. In Japan and Scotland, a black cat means good luck.
beats.loop_say: So it depends on your map. Because
beats.short_title: Black Cats Are Good Luck in Japan and Scotland 🐈‍⬛
beats.bonus: In Scotland, a strange black cat on your doorstep is said to bring prosperity.
beats.comment: Good luck or bad luck where you live? 👇
sources: Cats Protection (UK), black cat superstitions (lucky in Japan and the UK; crossing your path is good luck) — https://www.cats.org.uk/cats-blog/black-cat-superstitions
Catster, are black cats good luck (Scotland doorstep = prosperity; Japan good luck) — https://www.catster.com/lifestyle/are-black-cats-good-luck
Caveat (Fact desk): folklore varies by region; the script says 'in parts of England', not 'in the UK'.
Photos: domestic cats, CC0/CC BY; 206822105 is a pet indoors (casual grade, species not in doubt).

beats.say: In parts of England, one crossing your path is lucky too.
And cats are hunters. They pounce on small, round things that roll.
Small. Round. Rolls. I don't love it.
Luck: good. For meatballs: unclear.
Crows really do gather around a dead crow. But it's not a funeral. It's a lesson about danger.
beats.loop_say: And they remember faces. So, quick reminder:
beats.short_title: Crows Really Do Gather Around Their Dead 🐦‍⬛
beats.bonus: Crows ignored a dead pigeon. Only a dead crow set them off.
beats.comment: Has a crow ever held a grudge against you? 👇
sources: Swift & Marzluff 2015, Animal Behaviour 109:187-197, 'Wild American crows gather around their dead to learn about danger' (mob dead crows; scold the associated person; slower to approach food there; association up to 6 weeks; dead pigeon no effect) — https://corvidresearch.blog/2015/09/26/why-crows-gather-around-their-dead/
NYT / Carl Zimmer, 1 Oct 2015, crows may learn lessons from death — https://carlzimmer.com/crows-may-learn-lessons-from-death-88/
Framing rule: 'not a funeral' (the study measured threat learning, not grief).

beats.say: In a study, crows scolded the person holding a dead crow, and avoided food at that spot.
That grudge lasted up to six weeks.
They also eat almost anything. Including leftovers. I am leftovers.
Not a funeral. A safety meeting.
Owls aren't omens of death. But they really can fly almost without a sound.
beats.loop_say: You won't hear it coming. That's the point. Anyway,
beats.short_title: Owls Aren't Death Omens, But They Can Fly in Silence 🦉
beats.bonus: Engineers have copied the owl's feather comb to make wind turbines quieter.
beats.comment: Have you ever heard an owl fly over? 👇
sources: Audubon, 'The Silent Flight of Owls, Explained' (leading-edge comb, velvety surface, trailing fringe) — https://www.audubon.org/magazine/silent-flight-of-owls-explained
Knowable Magazine, how owls fly without making a sound — https://knowablemagazine.org/article/technology/2020/how-owls-fly-without-making-a-sound
Payne & Drury 1958; Payne 1971; Konishi (barn owls strike prey in total darkness by sound alone) — https://www.americanscientist.org/node/2084
Omen claim is folklore, not biology; script corrects it and moves to the true spooky fact.

beats.say: Comb-like edges on its feathers break up the air, and a velvety surface soaks up the sound.
Barn owls can catch mice in total darkness, just by listening.
Silent. Hunts at night. Likes small, round things. Lights on.
Omen: no. Stealth: yes.
No spider lays its eggs in your skin. There's no real case in medical records. Not one.
beats.loop_say: So you can relax. Mostly. Because
beats.short_title: No Spider Lays Eggs in Your Skin (Here's Where They Go) 🕷️
beats.bonus: The legend may trace partly to a 1982 horror novel, but it's older than that.
beats.comment: Who told you this one as a kid? 👇
sources: Burke Museum spider myths (Rod Crawford), 'Myth: Baby spiders from bite wounds' / eggs under skin: no real case in scientific or medical literature — https://www.burkemuseum.org/collections-and-research/biology/arachnology-and-entomology/spider-myths/myth-baby-spiders-bite
Wolf spiders (Lycosidae, incl. Pardosa) carry the egg sac attached to the spinnerets; widows guard egg sacs in the web — https://www.burkemuseum.org/static/spidermyth/
Photos: Pardosa lugubris with egg sac (369498853), Latrodectus hesperus with egg sac (10679778).

beats.say: Spiders wrap their eggs in a silk sac. This wolf spider tows hers behind her.
A black widow guards her egg sac in her web.
They're great parents. I was raised by a frying pan.
Eggs in skin: myth. Eggs in silk: fact.
